scope: The rules that moved the terms for foreign capital into Indian listed markets (SEBI FPI regulations 2017-2026), the two treaty amendments that reset the tax base for treaty-routed capital (Mauritius, Singapore, 2016), the P-Notes/ODI, ECB and Press Note 3 regimes, GIFT City's fund-management incentives, and the Budget 2024 capital-gains change — plus the regulators themselves (SEBI chairs Tyagi/Buch/Pandey, RBI governors Das/Malhotra, FM Sitharaman, DEA/DIPAM secretaries) with date-ranged roles, and a calibrated read of the Hindenburg-vs-Buch conflict-of-interest allegation through its denial, the Lokpal's 2025 closure and the Bombay HC's separate, unrelated FIR-stay proceeding. Leaves out: named FPI/adviser holders and mandates (research/raw/capital/holders.json, mandates-ventures.json), the underlying Adani-Hindenburg market-manipulation allegations and SEBI's September 2025 orders on them (already in the Atlas as energy:doc-sebi-adani-orders-2025 / energy:doc-hindenburg-adani-2023 — referenced, not duplicated), and World Bank/IMF project lending (research/raw/finance/worldbank-projects.json).

entities.label: Foreign Portfolio Investors registered with SEBI (Category I/II)
entities.sub: The class of entities registered under the SEBI (FPI) Regulations — the governed class for every FPI rule in this file, not a single node
entities.publicRole: The regulatory subject-class of every FPI rule change recorded here.
d: SEBI (FPI) Regulations, 2019 define two categories: Category I (govt./govt.-related, incl. sovereign wealth funds, central banks, multilateral agencies, pension/university funds meeting conditions) and Category II (all other registered FPIs) [documented]

entities.label: Indian entities eligible to raise External Commercial Borrowings
entities.sub: The class of Indian corporates, NBFCs, ports, infrastructure and start-up borrowers governed by the RBI's ECB framework — not a single node
entities.publicRole: The regulatory subject-class of the RBI's ECB liberalisations recorded here.
d: RBI Master Direction on ECB, Trade Credit and Structured Obligations, 26 March 2019, consolidated the four-category (limits/purpose/track/currency) ECB regime into one framework with automatic-route limits [documented]

entities.label: Investors (FDI and beneficial owners) from countries sharing a land border with India
entities.sub: The class governed by Press Note 3 of 2020 and its 2026 easing — China, Pakistan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Nepal, Bhutan, Afghanistan — not a single node
entities.publicRole: The regulatory subject-class of Press Note 3 (2020) and its 2026 amendment.
d: DPIIT Press Note 3 (17 April 2020) requires prior government approval for all FDI, direct or indirect (incl. beneficial-ownership changes), from entities of any country sharing a land border with India [documented]
srcs: Bar and Bench — Curbs on foreign investment by China: An analysis of Press Note 3

entities.label: SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019
entities.sub: Notified 23 September 2019, replacing the 2014 FPI Regulations; simplified three FPI categories into two and removed the 'broad-based' registration condition for Category II
entities.publicRole: The base statute governing every FPI registered in India through this file's period.
d: Review initiated by SEBI in March 2018 under a committee chaired by Harun R. Khan (former RBI Deputy Governor); committee report published 24 May 2019; regulations notified 23 September 2019, effective for new registrations and grandfathered existing FPIs [documented]

Collapsed the pre-2019 three-tier FPI category structure into two: Category I (govt./govt.-related, low-risk) and Category II (all other registered FPIs, incl. the individual funds central to the Adani-FPI dispute) [documented]
srcs: Mondaq/Bhatt & Joshi Associates — SEBI FPI Regulations 2019: A Comprehensive Analysis

entities.label: SEBI FPI 'broad-based fund' amendment, 2018
entities.sub: SEBI board decision (Jan 2018) and subsequent circular easing access norms for FPIs, dropping the requirement that a Category II ('broad-based') fund have at least 20 investors with none holding more than 49%
entities.publicRole: The specific 2018 easing that later FPI-transparency rules (2023-25) were built to counteract.
d: SEBI board paper 'Easing of Access Norms for Investment by Foreign Portfolio Investors', Jan 2018, proposed removing the fixed 20-investor floor for 'broad-based' Category II funds, allowing open-ended funds to keep the classification even if investor count fell, provided remaining investors were banks, sovereign funds or other institutional investors [documented]

The SC-appointed expert committee (2023) and Hindenburg Research (2023) both later identified small, concentrated FPIs with narrow investor bases among the entities holding Adani group shares as the specific structural gap this kind of easing left open [reported]
srcs: SEBI board paper — Easing of Access Norms for Investment by Foreign Portfolio Investors, Jan 2018

entities.label: India-Mauritius DTAA, 3rd Protocol (2016)
entities.sub: Protocol signed 10 May 2016 giving India source-based taxing rights over capital gains on Indian shares held via Mauritius from 1 April 2017, with pre-2017 acquisitions grandfathered and FY2017-19 gains taxed at 50% of the domestic rate
entities.publicRole: The single largest change to the treaty-shopping route historically used by round-tripped and legitimate FPI/PE capital alike.
d: Protocol signed 10 May 2016; capital gains on shares acquired before 1 April 2017 remain fully exempt in India regardless of sale date ('grandfathered'); gains on shares acquired on/after 1 April 2017 taxed at 50% of the domestic rate until 31 March 2019, then the full domestic rate [documented]
srcs: K&L Gates — Investing in India? Take a Look at the Amended India-Mauritius Tax Treaty

entities.label: India-Singapore DTAA, 3rd Protocol (2016)
entities.sub: Protocol signed 30 December 2016, mirroring the Mauritius protocol's move from residence-based to source-based capital-gains taxation, with the same grandfathering and transition schedule
entities.publicRole: Closed the same treaty-shopping route via Singapore, contemporaneous with the Mauritius amendment.
d: Signed 30 December 2016; the Singapore treaty's capital-gains exemption had itself been contingent on the Mauritius treaty (the 2005 Singapore protocol's benefits were pegged to Mauritius's), so amending Mauritius first made a parallel Singapore amendment necessary to avoid a sudden Singapore-only loophole [documented]
srcs: CMS Law — India and Singapore amend tax treaty

entities.label: SEBI Participatory Note (ODI) restrictions, 2016-2017
entities.sub: SEBI board decision (10 June 2016) requiring FPI issuers to KYC all P-Note/ODI subscribers including UBOs above 10%, followed by a 7 July 2017 circular banning P-Notes for equity derivatives
entities.publicRole: Tightened the least-transparent FPI sub-channel, prompted by the Special Investigation Team (SIT) on black money.
d: SEBI board, 10 June 2016, approved requiring ODI issuers to obtain and maintain full KYC on ODI/P-Note subscribers (incl. UBOs holding over 10%) and to file suspicious-transaction reports with India's Financial Intelligence Unit; circular of 7 July 2017 went further and banned P-Notes for investing in equity derivatives outright, citing the SIT on black money's recommendations [documented]
srcs: Angel One — Rules of Participatory Notes (P-Note), SEBI

entities.label: RBI External Commercial Borrowings (ECB) Master Direction, 2019, and 2022 liberalisation
entities.sub: Consolidated ECB framework of 26 March 2019 (automatic-route limit USD 750m/year, tiered all-in-cost ceilings) temporarily liberalised 1 Aug 2022 (limit doubled to USD 1.5bn, ceilings raised 100bps) for ECBs availed to 31 Dec 2022
entities.publicRole: The rulebook for foreign-currency debt into Indian companies, distinct from the FPI-equity rules that are the rest of this file.
d: Master Direction issued 26 March 2019: automatic-route ECBs capped at USD 750m/entity/year; all-in-cost ceilings of benchmark+450 to +550bps depending on currency and vintage [documented]

1 August 2022 circular, implementing a 6 July 2022 RBI press release liberalising forex flows amid rupee depreciation, doubled the automatic-route limit to USD 1.5bn and raised all-in-cost ceilings by 100bps for investment-grade borrowers, for ECBs raised up to 31 December 2022 [documented]
srcs: Lexology — RBI temporarily raises all-in-cost ceiling and automatic-route borrowing limit for ECBs

entities.label: Press Note 3 of 2020 (DPIIT)
entities.sub: Issued 17 April 2020, requiring prior government approval for all FDI, direct or indirect (incl. a change of beneficial ownership), from an entity of any country sharing a land border with India, or where the beneficial owner is situated in or a citizen of such a country
entities.publicRole: The rule that made China-linked FDI and, by extension, China-domiciled FPI capital, a government-approval case rather than an automatic-route one.
d: Issued by DPIIT 17 April 2020, days after China's central bank (PBoC) raised its stake in HDFC Ltd to 1.01% amid a COVID-driven fall in Indian equity valuations; covers FDI, FPI and any other foreign investment where ultimate beneficial ownership traces to a land-bordering country, with no minimum threshold [documented]
srcs: Bar and Bench — Curbs on foreign investment by China: An analysis of Press Note 3

entities.label: Press Note 2 of 2026 (DPIIT) — Press Note 3 easing
entities.sub: Cabinet-approved 10 March 2026, DPIIT notification 15 March 2026: land-border-country investors may now hold up to 10% non-controlling stakes via the automatic route (subject to sectoral caps and a formal beneficial-ownership test), plus a 60-day fast-track approval track for named manufacturing sub-sectors
entities.publicRole: The most consequential 2024-26 easing in this file's period, reversing part of Press Note 3 (2020) after six years.
d: Union Cabinet approved the amendment 10 March 2026; DPIIT's Press Note 2 (2026) followed 15 March 2026; introduces a formal 'beneficial ownership' definition, an automatic route for non-controlling stakes up to 10% subject to sectoral caps, and a 60-day expedited-approval track for capital goods, electronic capital goods, electronic components, polysilicon and ingot-wafer manufacturing [reported]

India Cellular and Electronics Association (ICEA) president Pankaj Mohindroo and India Electronics and Semiconductor Association (IESA) president Ashok Chandak publicly welcomed the change as enabling faster technology partnerships and non-strategic Chinese capital into electronics manufacturing — the two industry bodies whose members are the PLI-scheme electronics/solar manufacturers most dependent on Chinese equipment and component suppliers [reported]
srcs: BDO India — India eases FDI rules under Press Note 3 with 10% cap for border-country investors

entities.label: IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2022, and GIFT-IFSC fund tax incentives
entities.sub: IFSCA's 2022 regulatory framework for Fund Management Entities at GIFT City, paired with a Section 80LA-style profit-linked tax holiday and GST/STT exemptions for units doing business from the IFSC
entities.publicRole: The onshore-offshore hybrid route through which global asset managers (incl. BlackRock-Jio, per the holders file) now book some India-linked fund activity.
d: IFSCA (Fund Management) Regulations, 2022 created three Fund Management Entity categories — Registered FME (non-retail, investors with min. net worth USD 75,000), Registered FME (retail, min. USD 500,000) and Authorised FME (large managers, min. USD 5m) [reported]

GIFT-IFSC units get a 100% profit-linked tax exemption for 10 of a 15-year block, plus GST and Securities Transaction Tax exemption on IFSC-exchange transactions and pass-through tax treatment for the fund vehicle itself [reported]
srcs: India Briefing — GIFT City: India's Rising Star for Foreign Portfolio Investors

entities.label: Union Budget 2024-25 — capital-gains tax increase (incl. FPIs)
entities.sub: Finance (No.2) Act 2024, effective 23 July 2024: LTCG on listed equity up from 10% to 12.5%, STCG up from 15% to 20%, both rates applying identically to FPIs taxed under Income-tax Act s.115AD
entities.publicRole: The one FPI rule change in this file that is a clear tightening, not an easing, and applies without distinguishing FPI nationality or size.
d: Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman's Budget 2024-25 (presented 23 July 2024) raised long-term capital-gains tax on listed equity from 10% to 12.5% and short-term capital-gains tax from 15% to 20%, effective transfers from 23 July 2024; the equity LTCG exemption threshold was raised from Rs 1 lakh to Rs 1.25 lakh in the same Budget [documented]

Income-tax Act s.115AD taxes FPIs' capital gains on listed securities at the same rates as resident taxpayers under s.111A/112A, so the 2024 hike applied to FPI portfolios without a separate notification [reported]
srcs: Kotak Mutual Fund — Mutual Fund Taxation (FY 2024-25): Equity, Debt, SIP & IDCW
Business Standard (via search) — Budget 2024 hikes LTCG tax rate to 12.5%, STCG to 20%

entities.label: SEBI FPI granular-disclosure size threshold raised to Rs 50,000 crore (2025)
entities.sub: SEBI board (209th meeting, 24 March 2025) approved doubling the Aug-2023 size criterion from Rs 25,000 crore to Rs 50,000 crore equity AUM, citing a more-than-doubling of cash-market trading volumes since FY2022-23; the 50%-single-group-concentration criterion was left unchanged
entities.publicRole: The first major relaxation of the Aug-2023 post-Hindenburg disclosure regime, roughly 19 months after that regime took effect.
d: SEBI's 209th board meeting, 24 March 2025 (PR No.15/2025), approved raising the size-based granular-disclosure threshold from Rs 25,000 crore to Rs 50,000 crore equity AUM in Indian markets, citing cash-equity trading volumes having more than doubled between FY2022-23 (when the original limit was set) and FY2024-25 [documented]

The board explicitly retained, unchanged, the separate criterion catching any FPI with over 50% of its India equity AUM concentrated in a single corporate group — the criterion under which the Adani-linked FPIs were originally identified [reported]
Sovereign wealth funds and public/government-related (Category I) funds remained exempt from the size-based disclosure requirement, as they had been since the August 2023 circular [reported]
srcs: BusinessToday — FPI threshold limit to make additional disclosures raised to Rs 50,000 crore in equity AUM: Sebi
Business Upturn — SEBI retains rule mandating additional disclosures by FPIs holding over 50% equity AUM in a single corporate group

entities.label: SEBI circular exempting University Funds/Endowments from granular FPI disclosure (Aug 2024)
entities.sub: Circular of 1 August 2024 exempting Category I FPIs that are university funds or university-related endowments from the Aug-2023 granular beneficial-ownership disclosure requirement, subject to conditions on India-AUM concentration, global AUM size and tax-exempt non-profit status
entities.publicRole: One of the two named carve-outs (with sovereign/pension funds) from the post-Hindenburg disclosure regime.
d: SEBI circular, 1 August 2024, exempts Category I FPIs that are university funds/university-related endowments from the granular look-through disclosure of the August 2023 circular, conditional on: India-equity AUM under 25% of the fund's global AUM; global AUM over Rs 10,000 crore; and a filed return showing tax-exempt non-profit status in the home jurisdiction [reported]
srcs: EY India — Additional disclosure framework for Foreign Portfolio Investors: SEBI consultation paper

entities.label: SEBI exemption for FPIs concentrated in a listed company with no identified promoter (March 2024)
entities.sub: Circular following the 15 March 2024 SEBI board meeting, exempting an FPI from the 50%-single-group granular-disclosure trigger where the concentration is in a listed company that has no identified promoter, subject to a 3%-of-total-equity composite cap
entities.publicRole: A control case for the symmetry check: a facially neutral rule whose beneficiaries are, by its own drafting, companies without a promoter group to hide — the opposite structural profile from the one Hindenburg alleged of Adani group companies.
d: SEBI board meeting 15 March 2024 approved exempting FPIs from the 50%-concentration disclosure trigger where the concentrated holding is in a listed company with no identified promoter, provided the FPI's holding (excluding the no-promoter company) stays under 50% of its India AUM and all such FPIs' composite holding in the no-promoter company stays under 3% of its total equity; rationale given was that Minimum Public Shareholding concerns do not arise absent an identifiable promoter who could indirectly hold shares via the FPI [reported]
srcs: MoneyLife — SEBI Proposes Increasing Threshold for FPIs' Granular Disclosures to Rs 50,000 Crore

entities.label: SEBI High-Level Committee on Conflict of Interest, Disclosures and Related Matters (2025)
entities.sub: Constituted per the 24 March 2025 board decision, announced by PR No.85/2025 (9 April 2025); chaired by Injeti Srinivas, with Uday Kotak, G. Mahalingam, Sarit Jaffa and R. Narayanaswamy as members, to review conflict-of-interest, asset/liability disclosure and insider-trading-definition rules for SEBI's own Members and officials
entities.publicRole: SEBI's own institutional response to the August 2024 Hindenburg allegations against its then chairperson.
d: Constituted following the SEBI board meeting of 24 March 2025 — the same meeting that raised the FPI disclosure threshold — and formally announced by SEBI PR No.85/2025 on 9 April 2025; composition: Injeti Srinivas (Vice-Chairman), Uday Kotak, G. Mahalingam, Sarit Jaffa, R. Narayanaswamy [documented]

The board later approved recommendations requiring the SEBI Chairperson and Whole-Time Members to publicly disclose assets, liabilities and investments, and to be brought within the regulatory definition of 'insider' [reported]
srcs: SEBI — SEBI constitutes High-Level Committee on Conflict of Interest, Disclosures and related matters (PR No.85/2025)

entities.label: Supreme Court-appointed Expert Committee on SEBI's Adani/Hindenburg investigation (2023)
entities.sub: Constituted by SC order 2 March 2023, chaired by Justice A.M. Sapre (retd.), with O.P. Bhatt, Justice J.P. Devadhar (retd.), K.V. Kamath, Nandan Nilekani and Somasekhar Sundaresan; reported to the Supreme Court 6 May 2023
entities.publicRole: The judicial-process check on SEBI's own regulatory conduct during the Adani-Hindenburg episode — the immediate precursor to the August 2023 disclosure circular.
d: Constituted by Supreme Court order dated 2 March 2023; found it could not, on the material before it, conclude there had been 'regulatory failure' by SEBI in handling the alleged securities-law contraventions; said SEBI's pursuit of ultimate-beneficial-owner identification for 13 Adani-linked FPIs risked being 'a journey without a destination'; flagged six entities (including four FPIs) for suspicious pre-report trading in Adani group shares [reported]
srcs: LiveLaw — Adani-Hindenburg Report: Prima Facie 'No Regulatory Failure,' Says Supreme Court Expert Committee About SEBI Probe

entities.label: SEBI enhanced/granular FPI disclosure norms, Aug 2023
entities.sub: Circular of 24 August 2023 requiring full look-through beneficial-ownership disclosure from FPIs meeting either a 50%-of-AUM single-group-concentration test or a Rs 25,000 crore India-equity-AUM size test
entities.publicRole: The regulatory response, by SEBI, to the concern that opaque FPI structures can mask ultimate beneficial ownership -- reused verbatim from research/raw/capital/holders.json, which first defined this id; this file adds the rule's later amendment history (2024 exemptions, 2025 threshold increase) and its 'who asked / who benefited' reading.
d: 24 August 2023 circular applied from 1 November 2023: full look-through UBO disclosure, no minimum threshold, annual refresh, 7-working-day update on material change, with a 90-day re-alignment window for FPIs to fall below the trigger instead of disclosing [reported]

Amended three times in this file's period: 15 March 2024 (no-identified-promoter exemption), 1 August 2024 (university-fund exemption) and 24 March 2025 (size threshold Rs 25,000cr -> Rs 50,000cr) -- see the three linked law claims below
srcs: TaxGuru -- SEBI Tightens FPI Disclosure Norms after Adani-Hindenburg

entities.label: IPE Plus Fund 1
entities.sub: Mauritius-domiciled fund vehicle named in Hindenburg Research's 10 August 2024 report as the structure in which Madhabi Puri Buch and her husband Dhaval Buch held an investment made in 2015
entities.publicRole: The specific financial vehicle at the centre of the alleged Buch/Adani conflict-of-interest claim — named here only because the allegation itself, sourced to a named party (Hindenburg) and carrying the Buchs' contra, requires an addressable object.
d: Named by Hindenburg Research's 10 August 2024 report as a Mauritius-domiciled fund in which the Buchs held a stake made in 2015, two years before Madhabi Puri Buch joined SEBI as a whole-time member (2017) and seven years before she became Chairperson (2022); Hindenburg linked the fund's other investors to an associate of Vinod Adani [alleged, per Hindenburg]

d: 25th RBI Governor; assumed charge 12 December 2018 succeeding Urjit Patel; completed a six-year term (initial three years plus a three-year extension) and demitted office 10 December 2024.

d: 26th RBI Governor; Appointments Committee of the Cabinet approved 9 December 2024; took charge 11 December 2024 for a three-year term, succeeding Shaktikanta Das; previously Revenue Secretary, Ministry of Finance.
srcs: NewsOnAir (govt.) — Sanjay Malhotra appointed as new RBI Governor

d: Replaced the 2014 FPI Regulations; simplified three FPI risk categories into two; removed the 'broad-based' condition for Category II registration (continuing the 2018 easing, entry below); grew out of a 2018 committee (Harun R. Khan) explicitly framed as easing market access, not tightening it.

Boring explanation: most of the 2019 rewrite consolidated years of accumulated circulars and FAQs into one instrument, a housekeeping exercise SEBI does periodically for every registrant class, not an Adani-specific or FPI-specific favour.
srcs: Mondaq/Bhatt & Joshi Associates — SEBI FPI Regulations 2019: A Comprehensive Analysis

d: Removed the fixed 20-investor floor for a Category II fund to keep its 'broad-based' label, provided remaining investors are banks, sovereign funds or institutional investors.

Boring explanation: open-ended funds' investor counts fluctuate constantly; a hard 20-investor floor forced funds to re-register or restructure for a technical breach unrelated to actual risk. The change served the large majority of genuinely diversified FPIs with no Indian promoter link.
srcs: SEBI board paper — Easing of Access Norms for Investment by Foreign Portfolio Investors, Jan 2018

claims.lab: Cui bono: who the 2018 broad-based easing structurally favoured
d: The 2018 removal of a minimum-investor floor is the specific rule the 2023 SC expert committee and Hindenburg both point to when explaining how a handful of FPIs could remain classified as ordinary diversified funds while holding shares almost exclusively in one Indian corporate group, without a natural-person UBO ever surfacing.
srcs: LiveLaw — Adani-Hindenburg Report: Prima Facie 'No Regulatory Failure', Says SC Expert Committee

benefit.how: a looser 'broad-based' floor made it structurally easier for a small number of concentrated, low-transparency FPI vehicles (per Hindenburg's contested 2023 allegation) to remain registered while holding shares overwhelmingly in Adani group companies, without a natural-person beneficial owner ever being disclosed, 2018-2023

claims.innocentReading: The 2018 change served the large majority of FPIs, which have nothing to do with any single Indian promoter group and whose investor counts fluctuate for ordinary commercial reasons; it was recommended years before the Adani allegations existed and was never targeted at any one issuer or group.
claims.upgradeIf: A regulator or court makes a specific finding that named 2018-registered FPIs were beneficially owned by an Adani-group promoter or associate.
claims.killIf: SEBI's or a court's investigation affirmatively identifies and discloses the natural-person beneficial owners of the 13 scrutinised FPIs and finds no Adani-promoter linkage.

d: Ended the pre-2017 zero-capital-gains-tax route via Mauritius on a going-forward basis, while grandfathering every share acquired before 1 April 2017 — so the single biggest winners of the 2016 amendment were the FPIs, PE funds and holding companies that had already routed capital through Mauritius before the deadline, who keep the old exemption on those specific shares indefinitely.

Boring explanation: the amendment was driven by a decade of Indian revenue-authority and CAG concern about treaty shopping and round-tripping via Mauritius (and, after 2016, an active base-erosion/BEPS-era international push against treaty abuse), not by any single investor's request.
srcs: K&L Gates — Investing in India? Take a Look at the Amended India-Mauritius Tax Treaty

d: Necessitated by the Mauritius amendment (the Singapore treaty's capital-gains exemption was contractually pegged to Mauritius's); same grandfathering and transition schedule, so pre-2017 Singapore-routed holdings kept the old exemption too.
srcs: CMS Law — India and Singapore amend tax treaty

d: Tightened the least-transparent FPI sub-channel (offshore derivative instruments/P-Notes) on the recommendation of the government's own Special Investigation Team on black money — a tightening driven by an anti-money-laundering mandate, not an industry request.
srcs: Angel One — Rules of Participatory Notes (P-Note), SEBI

claims.lab: RBI ECB Master Direction 2019 and 2022 liberalisation
d: 2019 consolidation was a housekeeping simplification; the August 2022 liberalisation (higher automatic-route limit, looser cost ceilings) was an explicit, time-boxed response to rupee depreciation and capital outflows after the US Fed's 2022 rate-hike cycle, not a request from any single borrower class — it lapsed by its own terms at end-2022.
srcs: Lexology — RBI temporarily raises all-in-cost ceiling and automatic-route borrowing limit for ECBs

d: Issued days after China's central bank raised its HDFC Ltd stake amid a COVID-driven valuation crash; explicit national-security/opportunistic-takeover rationale, applied to all land-border countries though China was the proximate trigger.
This claim's supersededBy points to the 2026 partial easing (below).

voids.what: SEBI has never published the names of the FPIs or the corporate groups (other than the Adani group) that triggered the August 2023 50%-single-group-concentration or Rs 25,000/50,000 crore size criteria.
voids.whyItMatters: Without this, the 'same lens on domestic promoters/other groups' symmetry check the brief asks for can only be assessed at the aggregate level (SEBI's own stated design intent and reported totals), not verified against named non-Adani cases — so the claim that the rule is genuinely group-neutral in practice, not just in drafting, cannot be independently tested from public sources.

voids.what: No public conflict-of-interest or recusal register existed for SEBI's Chairperson and Whole-Time Members before the March-April 2025 High-Level Committee process; SEBI's Sept 2025 Adani orders and the Lokpal's May 2025 order both had to reconstruct Buch's financial disclosures from what she volunteered, not from a standing public register.
voids.whyItMatters: The absence of a contemporaneous, auditable recusal record is exactly the gap that makes the Hindenburg-Buch allegation both hard to prove and hard to fully dismiss from outside records; the 2025 committee exists to fill this gap prospectively, not retrospectively.

narratives.claim: Hindenburg's August 2024 allegations show SEBI's own chairperson had a financial conflict of interest that let her go easy on the Adani investigation.
narratives.strongestCase: Buch and her husband are alleged to have held an undisclosed stake in a Mauritius fund structure Hindenburg tied to an associate of Vinod Adani; SEBI did not publish a recusal record showing she stayed out of Adani-specific matters; the timeline (2015 investment, 2017 SEBI appointment, 2022 chairpersonship, Adani probe from 2023) at minimum created an optics problem SEBI's own March 2025 conflict-of-interest committee was set up to address going forward.
narratives.strongestCounter: The investment was made in 2015, two years before she joined SEBI in any capacity, and in a private capacity before any regulatory role existed to create a conflict; the Lokpal's 28 May 2025 order, after reviewing three separate complaints including one from an opposition MP, found no prima facie case of corruption or quid pro quo and called the allegations unverified presumption; the underlying Adani short-selling allegations themselves were dismissed by SEBI's final orders in September 2025 (see atlas: energy:doc-sebi-adani-orders-2025) after the Supreme Court's own expert committee (May 2023) and judgment (Jan 2024) had already found no regulatory failure; a March 2025 FIR matter sometimes conflated with this allegation (Cals Refineries listing fraud, 1994) is a different case entirely, about a different set of facts, stayed by the Bombay HC on its merits.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Disclosure of SEBI's internal recusal log (if one exists) for Adani-related board/enforcement decisions during Buch's tenure; a Lokpal or court finding, rather than a dismissal on procedural/evidentiary grounds, that establishes an actual quid pro quo; independent confirmation (not yet found) of the alleged consultancy-income stream.
srcs: LiveLaw — Lokpal dismisses complaints against Buch

narratives.claim: SEBI eased FPI disclosure rules under industry pressure in 2024-25, quietly undoing the post-Hindenburg transparency reform.
narratives.strongestCase: The size threshold was doubled (Rs 25,000cr to Rs 50,000cr) within about 19 months of the original circular taking effect; university funds got a named exemption in August 2024; a further carve-out for no-identified-promoter companies arrived in March 2024; the pattern echoes the 2018 removal of the broad-based-fund floor, which itself made the kind of opaque, concentrated FPI Hindenburg later complained about easier to register in the first place — a repeating cycle of tighten-after-scandal, loosen-after-attention-fades.
narratives.strongestCounter: SEBI explicitly retained, unchanged, the one criterion that actually caught the Adani-linked FPIs — the 50%-single-group-concentration test — even while raising the size threshold; its stated reason for the size change (cash-market trading volumes more than doubling FY23-FY25) is a real, checkable market fact, not merely an assertion; the university-fund exemption carries hard conditions (India AUM under 25% of global AUM, tax-exempt status) rather than a blanket carve-out; and the same March 2025 board meeting that eased the size threshold also stood up the conflict-of-interest committee that tightened disclosure obligations on SEBI's own leadership — inconsistent with a simple 'protect insiders' reading of the meeting as a whole.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A disclosed lobbying submission from a specific FPI, custodian or industry body naming the threshold as the ask; evidence the concentration-test enforcement lapsed in practice after March 2025; a public breakdown, by SEBI, of which groups (beyond Adani) were caught by either criterion before and after the changes.
srcs: BusinessToday — FPI threshold limit to make additional disclosures raised to Rs 50,000 crore
Business Upturn — SEBI retains rule mandating additional disclosures for >50% single-group concentration

narratives.claim: The 2016 Mauritius/Singapore treaty amendments and their grandfathering clauses were designed to let round-tripped money that had already entered India via those routes escape the new source-taxation rules, while only closing the door on new entrants.
narratives.strongestCase: The grandfathering clause is, mechanically, exactly what a beneficiary of the old regime would want: every rupee of capital gain on shares acquired before 1 April 2017 via Mauritius (or Singapore) keeps the old zero/low-tax treatment forever, regardless of when it is eventually sold — a permanent, dated cutoff that protects existing positions while taxing only future ones.
narratives.strongestCounter: Grandfathering existing positions while changing the rule prospectively is the near-universal international norm for treaty and tax-law transitions (used, for example, in India's own retrospective-tax climbdown after the Vodafone/Cairn disputes going the other way), precisely because it is considered basic legal-certainty practice, not a targeted favour; the amendment's core purpose — ending open-ended zero-tax treaty shopping — is a net tightening for all new capital after 2017, and applied identically to every investor using the route, round-tripped or not, with no mechanism to identify or exempt round-tripped money specifically either before or after 2017.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Evidence the 2015-16 negotiation was shaped by submissions from specific round-tripping beneficiaries rather than the documented anti-BEPS/anti-treaty-shopping policy process; data on what share of pre-2017 Mauritius-routed capital was subsequently identified as round-tripped by Indian tax or enforcement authorities.
srcs: K&L Gates — Investing in India? Take a Look at the Amended India-Mauritius Tax Treaty

symmetryCheck: The brief's control is 'the same disclosure lens on domestic promoters/other FPI-holding groups.' SEBI's own circulars and board minutes state the 50%-concentration and size criteria in group-neutral terms and were, on SEBI's account, triggered by roughly Rs 2.6 lakh crore of FPI AUM as of March 2023 (base rate above) — far more than Adani group companies alone could account for, implying other groups were caught. The March 2024 no-identified-promoter exemption is the clearest documented evidence the rule is built around promoter-linked concentration generically: it is drafted to exclude exactly the companies (those without an identifiable promoter) that structurally cannot present the round-tripping risk the whole regime targets, and by that same logic it cannot apply to Adani group companies, which do have identified promoters. Where the lens fails the symmetry test is transparency, not design: SEBI has never named which non-Adani groups or FPIs were caught, so the claim that the rule bites broadly cannot be verified against named cases from public sources — only inferred from the aggregate AUM figure and the rule's own neutral drafting. That gap cuts both ways: it is equally consistent with a genuinely broad, Adani-including-but-not-Adani-only regime, and with a regime that in practice concentrates its bite on the one group whose FPIs drew press and judicial attention. This file cannot resolve that from what SEBI has published.
